passages.t: The Servant called from the womb, a light for the nations
passages.happening:
Now the Servant speaks for himself, to the islands and the distant peoples. ‘The LORD called Me from the womb; from the body of My mother He named Me’ (verse 1). God made his mouth like a sharp sword and hid him like a polished arrow in his quiver (verse 2).

God said to him, ‘You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory’ (verse 3). But the Servant answers with discouragement. He says he has labored in vain and spent his strength for nothing, ‘yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God’ (verse 4).

The LORD formed him from the womb to bring Jacob back to God (verse 5). And God says that is not enough. ‘I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 48 ended with the command to leave Babylon. From here on, Cyrus and Babylon are not mentioned again. Two figures take the stage: the Servant of the LORD, and Zion, the ruined city pictured as a grieving mother. Cyrus could free captives from Babylon. The Servant's work goes further: to bring Israel back to God and to carry God's salvation to the ends of the earth.

These verses are the second of the four Servant Songs, as the scholar Bernhard Duhm named them. In the first song, in chapter 42, God spoke about the Servant. Here the Servant speaks himself, and he admits discouragement.

His weapons are a sword and an arrow, a warrior's tools kept ready for the right moment, but here they describe his mouth. His power is his word. Being called and named from the womb echoes the call of prophets such as Jeremiah, set apart before birth.
passages.later: Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, calls him ‘a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel’ (Luke 2:32). Paul and Barnabas apply verse 6 to their own mission: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth’ (Acts 13:47).
passages.hard:
The Servant is called Israel in verse 3, but he is sent to restore Israel in verses 5 and 6. Who is he?

Readers have answered in four main ways. Some see the nation of Israel, or a faithful remnant within it sent to the rest; verse 3 names him Israel, and nearly all ancient manuscripts have the word. Some see the prophet himself, who speaks in the first person, reports his call from the womb like Jeremiah, and feels his work has failed. Some see another individual of the prophet's time, or a future king. Christians, following the New Testament, see the Servant at last in the Messiah, Jesus.

Many interpreters combine these. The Servant is called Israel because he embodies what Israel was meant to be, and since the nation as a whole had failed its calling (42:18-25; 48:1-8), the role narrows to one who fulfills it and so restores the rest. The New Testament applies verse 6 both to Jesus (Luke 2:32) and to those who carry his message (Acts 13:47).
passages.asks: The Servant says he has labored in vain, and still leaves his reward with God. Ask where your own work feels wasted, and whether you can leave its verdict with God. And ask who you know in the distant places that the light is meant to reach.

passages.t: A covenant for the people, and captives coming home
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to the one ‘who was despised and abhorred by the nation’ (verse 7), the servant of rulers. Kings will see him and rise, and princes will bow down, because the LORD has chosen him (verse 7).

‘In the time of favor I will answer You, and in the day of salvation I will help You’ (verse 8). God will appoint him to be a covenant for the people, to restore the land and share out its empty inheritances (verse 8). He will say to the prisoners, Come out, and to those in darkness, Show yourselves (verse 9).

‘They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them’ (verse 10). God will lead them beside springs of water. He will turn the mountains into roads (verse 11). They will come from far away, from the north and the west, and from the land of Aswan (verse 12).

“Shout for joy, O heavens; rejoice, O earth; break forth in song, O mountains!” (verse 13). The LORD has comforted his people.
passages.hearers:
The Servant is despised now, but kings will bow before him. That reversal, from rejection to honor, is a thread that runs through all the Servant Songs and reaches its fullest form in chapter 53.

To be a covenant for the people repeats the words of 42:6. The return is pictured as a new exodus. The people are fed on the way, protected from the sun, and led to water, as Israel was in the wilderness.

Verse 12 names the land of Aswan. The Hebrew word is Sinim, and the Great Isaiah Scroll found at Qumran supports reading it as Syene, the old name of Aswan at Egypt's southern border. Some once took Sinim to mean China, a view now generally given up. A Jewish military colony lived on the island of Elephantine near Aswan in the Persian period, known from papyri of the fifth century BC. The exiles were scattered far, and the promise reaches all of them.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 8 and adds, “Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!” (2 Corinthians 6:2). Revelation echoes verse 10 for the redeemed before the throne: ‘Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst’ (Revelation 7:16).
passages.asks: God promises to say to people in darkness, Show yourselves. Ask whether there is part of your life still hiding in the dark. And ask what it would look like to believe that today is a time of favor.

passages.t: Zion forgotten? Engraved on God's palms
passages.happening:
Then Zion speaks. “The LORD has forsaken me; the Lord has forgotten me!” (verse 14).

God answers with the strongest picture he can find. ‘Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb?’ (verse 15). “Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!” (verse 15). ‘Behold, I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands; your walls are ever before Me’ (verse 16).

Her builders hurry back, and her destroyers leave (verse 17). She is to lift her eyes and look. Her children are gathering, and she will wear them like jewels, like a bride (verse 18). Her ruined land will be too small for its people (verse 19). The children born in her grief will say there is no room (verse 20).

Zion will ask in her heart who bore these children for her, since she was bereaved and barren, exiled and alone. Where did they come from (verse 21)?
passages.hearers:
Jerusalem lay in ruins after 587 or 586 BC, its walls broken and its people scattered. That is the ground of Zion's complaint. The exiles who later came back after Cyrus's decree found a small, struggling community, so a land too small for its people spoke straight into their emptiness.

The nursing mother was the strongest bond the ancient world knew. Babies were nursed for two or three years, and for a mother to forget her child was almost unthinkable. God says that even if the unthinkable happened, he would not forget.

To inscribe a name on the palms may reflect the custom of marking the hand with a name as a sign of belonging or remembrance, as in 44:5. The word forget appears four times in the dialogue. The repetition answers the exiles' deepest fear.
passages.later: A psalm prays with the same fear: ‘How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?’ (Psalm 13:1). Jesus uses a mother's love too, longing to gather Jerusalem's children ‘as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings’ (Matthew 23:37).
passages.asks: Zion says aloud that God has forgotten her, and God answers her. Ask whether you have ever said that to God, and whether you could. And ask what it means for you that God keeps his people's walls ever before him.

passages.t: The nations carry Zion's children home
passages.happening:
‘This is what the Lord GOD says’ (verse 22). He will lift his hand to the nations and raise his banner. They will bring Zion's sons in their arms and carry her daughters on their shoulders (verse 22). Kings will look after her children, and their queens will nurse them (verse 23). They will bow before her. Those who hope in the LORD will never be put to shame (verse 23).

‘Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered?’ (verse 24). Yes, says the LORD. Even the captives of the mighty will be taken back, and he will contend with those who contend with Zion and save her children (verse 25).

The chapter ends with a harsh picture of Zion's oppressors turning on themselves (verse 26). Then all people will know that the LORD is Zion's Savior and Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The empire had carried away Judah's children. Now the picture is reversed. The nations carry them home, and kings and queens care for them as if they were their own. The powerful will serve the people they once oppressed.

Verse 24 asks the question the exiles would ask: can anyone take captives back from a mighty empire? God answers that he will.

The last verse uses the language of siege warfare, where starving cities were driven to desperation. Here it is turned on the oppressors, to say they will destroy themselves. The poem names the picture in a line and moves on to its goal, that every people will know who saved Zion.
passages.later: A psalm sings of the return: ‘When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers’ (Psalm 126:1). Isaiah returns to the picture of nations bringing Zion's children home: ‘They will bring all your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the LORD’ (Isaiah 66:20).
passages.hard:
Kings lick the dust at Zion's feet, and oppressors destroy themselves. Is this a wish for revenge?

The pictures are the language of reversal, drawn from war and from the customs of kings. The empire that humbled Zion is humbled, and the tyrant's captives are taken back. The chapter gives the judgment to God, who contends with those who contend with Zion, and its goal is that all mankind will know the LORD as Savior (verse 26).

Nothing here gives any people a warrant to wish harm on another people now, or to read any nation's suffering as deserved.
passages.asks: The exiles asked whether a tyrant's captives could ever be set free. Ask what captivity in your life feels too strong to break. And ask what it would mean to hope in the LORD in a way that will not be put to shame.
